title: Chapter 15 – Nine Pins
html:
Old Nan has been lighting the kitchen stove with the same Fire Seed talisman for six weeks, and this morning it gives out.

Lin Jian watches it happen from the doorway. She sets the slip into the iron cradle under the pot, presses her thumb to the corner node, and murmurs the single word that wakes it. The circuit flickers orange, brightens, and gutters out like a candle in a draft. The pot stays cold. Old Nan looks at the dead slip, then at the sky through the window, as though one of them has let her down.

"That's the fifth one this month," she says to nobody. "They don't make them like they used to."

They do, actually. They make them better. Lin Jian has been quietly feeding the shop's paper through the new mill for two seasons, and he knows exactly how much Qi a cheap talisman holds and how long it takes to leak out through a rough fiber. The one in Old Nan's hand is from the old stock, the coarse brown paper that was all the family could afford before the winter. It was never going to last six weeks.

He slips a fresh one from his own sleeve, a Fire Seed in the new orange ink, and sets it in the cradle beside hers.

"Try this one."

She does. The circuit blooms to a steady amber glow, and a low even heat rolls up into the pot. Old Nan stares at it. Then she turns and looks at him with narrowed eyes, the way she looks at a pot she suspects of boiling over.

"Your father's work?"

"Yes."

"Hm," says Old Nan. She doesn't ask what he is doing carrying them around in his sleeve. It is one of the things Lin Jian has come to value about her. She has been feeding this family for fifty years, and she knows precisely which questions are worth the trouble.

He leaves her to her pot and goes out into the cold.

It has been nine days since the hollow.

The household has changed in nine days. It is not a visible change, the walls are the same, the terraces are the same, the smoke still goes up from the kitchen chimney in the morning. But the cousins no longer walk the paths alone. The guards on the wall carry their swords unsheathed, and every one of them has a Mirror Guard talisman pinned to the inside of his short robe, courtesy of Father, who has not slept more than three hours a night since the funeral. Third Aunt is back in her herb terraces, tending the winter beds with her hair coiled hard and her hands moving as if they belong to someone else. Nobody speaks to her about Bo. Nobody has to.

And in the council's long silence, there is a number. Nobody has said it aloud. Lin Jian has worked it out for himself, from the way the Patriarch stands at the north wall every evening and looks at the dark.

He will come back.

The man in the feather cloak. He lost an eye, or part of one. Feng's pepper saw to that. But Hu told them at the funeral, in the flat voice he uses for facts: a blood-drinker heals faster than any normal cultivator, and he doesn't forget. Ten days. Maybe twenty. Then he comes.

Twenty days, from the hollow. Nine are gone.

\ \ \*

"Pins," says Old Hu.

He is sitting on the floor of the forge with his back against the anvil and a leather roll across his knees. He unties it with his one hand and his teeth, and spreads it open on the dirt.

Nine slim spikes of dull gray metal lie in a row, each as long as a hand, each thicker than Lin Jian's thumb at the head and drawn to a needle point at the other end. Fine lines are etched down the length of each one in a tight spiral. They look like something a gardener might use to stake a tomato. They look like nothing at all.

"Mortal-high," says Hu. "Which means they'll work on anything up to the sixth layer if you don't ask too much of them. Spirit iron, cheap grade, drawn from the scrap in the granary. I've been making these for a month." He picks one up and turns it in the light. "Four of these make a binding. Six make a snare. Nine make a pit. You drive them into the ground in the right pattern, you feed them Qi, and the earth between them stops being earth for as long as the Qi lasts."

Lin Jian crouches. He doesn't touch. "Stops being earth?"

"Becomes soft. Heavy. Hungry." Hu grunts. "A man steps in, he sinks to the knee and then the thigh. The deeper he goes, the harder it grips. You want a prisoner, you use four. You want a beast on its back, six. You want a thing to stay where it falls," he drops the pin back into the roll, "nine."

"For how long?"

"A hundred breaths, if you feed it well. Less if the thing struggles." Hu looks at him. "And that's all it is, boy. A hundred breaths. Do not let anyone tell you a formation wins a fight. It buys you a hundred breaths. What you do with them is the fight."

Lin Jian nods slowly.

"Question," says Hu.

"Yes?"

"You went through my pin bag in the granary last month. Don't deny it. The nine-pin set. The flaw in the third pin. You pointed to it without being told." The old man's one eye is flat and patient. "How did you know?"

It is a trap, Lin Jian thinks, but a gentle one. The kind a master sets for a pupil he already half trusts.

"The spiral on the third pin is shallower," he says. "By about a hair. If the lines aren't even, the Qi pools at the thick end instead of running through. It would work, but it would work badly."

"A hair." Hu's mouth twitches under the gray beard. "Your father would call that an eye for line. Third Aunt would call it a nose for herbs. I'd call it something else, but I won't." He rolls the pins up again. "Here is what is going to happen. I am going to build a pit at the north trail, where the old road meets the gate. A proper one. Nine pins, set in daylight, in front of the guards, with the Patriarch watching. Every servant in this house is going to see it go in."

"A decoy."

Hu doesn't blink. "I said nothing about a decoy."

"You said every servant."

"I did." A slow breath. "And I said nothing about where the second pit is going."

Lin Jian waits.

"There's a gap in the north rim," says Hu, "where the quarry cuts down to the lower terraces. A man coming fast through the hollow, wounded and angry, would take it. It's the only way down that isn't thorn thicket." He taps the leather roll. "That's where the real one goes. At night, with the Patriarch and your mother, and nobody else. And you."

"Me?"

"I need a second pair of hands that can set a pin to a hair." Hu looks up. "And I need someone who'll tell me, afterward, whether I did it right."

\ \ \*

By the third night there are two pits.

The first is a stagecraft marvel: a broad shallow depression at the north trail, ringed with stakes and strung with warning cord, built in full view of the guard and the farm hands and a long line of children who have been told, firmly, to keep away. Hu drives the nine pins himself, one after the other, with a stone mallet and a great deal of grunting. It takes him the whole of one afternoon. He feeds the array at the end, a flat green pulse of Qi, and the earth in the center of the ring sags gently, like a pudding, and Fourth Uncle's biggest guard, who is a mortal and tests it with a spear, loses the spear to the knee.

There is applause. Hu bows, sourly.

The second is built in the dark.

It goes into the narrow gap in the north rim, the way the quarry cuts down to the lower terraces, a path just wide enough for a single running man. There are only five of them present: the Patriarch, who stands with his notched sword and says nothing; Su Qinghe, who watches the ridge with her knife in her hand; Hu, who drives the pins; Father, who has come with a dozen of his best Mirror Guard talismans to bury in the gravel; and Lin Jian, who holds the lantern.

The lantern is a Moonlamp, a bluish glow from a talisman pinned to a bamboo frame, giving off the soft cold radiance of a winter moon. It is one of the first talismans Father taught him. He holds it with his arm braced against his chest, and watches the old man work.

It is a lesson. He knows it is, and he watches it like one. How Hu measures the spacing by eye, forty strides to a pin, no more, no less. How he sets them in a ring, then a cross, then a spiral. How he tests each with the flat of his palm, feeling for something Lin Jian cannot feel. How the rod, the iron rod that has hung at his side since the hollow, comes down on each pin with the exact same force, so that the heads are level.

The last pin goes in. Hu pushes Qi into the ring, and the gravel between them shivers once, and goes still.

"Done," he says. "Now. Check it."

Lin Jian sets down the lantern. He kneels in the cold gravel at the edge of the ring, puts his palm flat on the ground, and scans.

```
[Scan: Nine-Pin Pit (Quarry Gap)]
Pins: 9, spirit iron (low grade)
Spiral depth: 6 pins nominal, 3 pins 0.4 mm shallow
Array coherence: 81%
Hold time (est.): 94 breaths vs. 600 lb. target
Weakest link: Pin 5 (northeast), spiral shallow, Qi leak 7%
```

Nothing he didn't know. Three of the pins have the same fault as the one in the granary: a groove that peters out, a hair too shallow. A hundred breaths becomes ninety-four. It is not a disaster.

But it is information, and he has one great advantage over every formation master who has ever lived: he knows exactly how much it will hold.

"Pin five leaks," he says quietly. "Northeast. A little."

Hu stares at him. Then at the pin. Then, slowly, he reaches down and pulls it out of the ground, tilts it to the Moonlamp, and runs his thumb down the spiral.

"Gods," he says softly. "I thought I'd cut that one clean."

He drives it back with a quarter turn. Lin Jian scans again.

```
[Scan: Nine-Pin Pit (Quarry Gap)]
Array coherence: 86%
Hold time (est.): 103 breaths
```

Better. Not perfect.

When the others have gone back up the hill, and the gravel has been raked smooth and the tell-tale marks scuffed away, Lin Jian stays a moment longer.

"I could cut them," he says to Hu, in a voice no one else can hear. "The pins. If you wanted. I could make you nine that are right."

The old man is silent for a long time.

"With what?"

"With a file and a good lamp." He does not look up. "Please don't ask me how."

"I wasn't going to." Hu's voice is odd. "I was going to say that if you can, you should. And that if you do, you'll have to make a mistake in every one of them. A little one. Enough that if anyone checks, they'll see a boy of eight who had a good day."

A flaw in everything, Lin Jian thinks. The easy part is making it right. The hard part is making it wrong.

"Seventy-eight percent," he says. "Not eighty-one. They'll see a boy who's good, not a boy who's something else."

Hu looks at him for a long moment in the blue lamplight, and he says, very low: "I'm going to pretend I didn't hear that."

\ \ \*

He makes the pins that night, in his room, by lamplight, with the door barred and the window covered.

Nine blanks of low-grade spirit iron lie on the desk in front of him, drawn from the scrap pile in the granary. He lays his hand on the first and opens the interface, and the panel unfolds in his mind, cool and clean.

```
[Fabrication: Nine-Pin Set]
Material: spirit iron (low), 9 blanks
Required: spiral groove (uniform depth 1.2 mm), tip hardening, Qi channel
Creation Energy cost: 18
Current CE: 27 / 400
Accuracy target: 99% — OR custom (flaw injection)
```

He feeds it the target. Not 99. Seventy-eight. And then, because a flaw is only a flaw if it looks like a flaw, he places the errors by hand: a shallow groove on the third pin, a slightly blunt tip on the sixth, a hairline kink in the Qi channel of the ninth. Small mistakes, the kind a good apprentice makes when he is tired. He studies the pattern for a moment, checking it for plausibility, the way a forger checks a signature.

Nine pins form in the air above the desk, one after another, in a soft gold glow. They settle onto the blotter, and he picks one up. It is warm. The spiral is perfect, except where it isn't.

Eighteen points, he thinks, looking at the panel. Nine pins. Two points each. He had thought it would be more. A fabrication that precise at Level 1 would have cost him a week's worth of Creation Energy. At Level 2 it is a lot cheaper. That is the thing nobody tells you about leveling up: it does not make anything possible. It makes things cheap.

He checks the pins against the panel's blueprint once more, and the flaws are exactly where he put them.

Then, because he is a careful person, he makes a tenth.

A single pin. No flaw. Ninety-nine percent. It lies on the blotter in the lamplight like a splinter of the moon, perfectly straight and perfectly even, and he turns it over in his fingers and thinks about what it would take to make nine of those. To fill a pit that held, not for a hundred breaths, but for three hundred. To buy, in a single stroke, enough time to turn a battle.

Not yet, he tells himself. Not until I know what I need them for.

He wraps the tenth pin in a cloth and puts it at the bottom of his desk.

\ \ \*

The breakthrough comes at the fourth hour after midnight, which he has not planned.

He has been sitting in the cold for most of the night with Third Aunt's recipe open in his mind and a pill on his tongue. A Breath-Gathering Pill, the new kind, ninety-six percent pure, brewed from the willow-mint and frost-cap and the salt-bark in the proportions he had worked out for her. He had not meant to take it. He had meant to leave it on the desk. But he had been awake for twenty hours, and his hands were shaking, and the old familiar bright spot under his ribs had started to throb, and he had known, in the way one knows a sneeze is coming, that something was about to happen.

The pill dissolves. The Qi pours in.

It is not like the other times. The first four layers had come through patience, grinding it out meridian by meridian, widening the road. This is a wall. Lin Jian can feel it, high in his chest, a great dense barrier that his Qi hits and slides off, hits and slides off. He pushes. It does not give.

Fourth layer to fifth, Mao had said, once, in the training yard, to a row of cousins. Everyone stalls here. It's where you learn how much of the road is still unfinished.

He pushes harder. The wall holds.

He thinks about the hollow. The crows over the north slope, the sound Lin Shu made coming up the trail, Third Aunt's face in the snow. He thinks about a hollow body on a long table. He thinks about nine pins and a hundred breaths. And somewhere in the back of his mind a small calm voice says: It isn't a wall. It's a door. You've been pushing on the hinge.

He stops pushing. He lets the Qi go still, and then very gently, off center, along the grain, the way he would work a stuck lid, he leans.

The door swings open.

The Qi rushes through, bright and enormous, and Lin Jian has time to think oh before it fills him to the edge. His meridians burn. His head rings. The room, the dark room, the desk, the lamp, goes razor-sharp, as if someone has wiped a window that had been dirty all his life, and he can feel the walls around him, the whole east wing, the sleeping bodies in their beds, a warm haze of small lights like fireflies in a field.

He sits on the floor with his back against the bed and breathes, and waits for it to settle.

```
[Status]
Qi Refining: Layer 5 (early)
Qi capacity: +38%
Spiritual sense: extended (est. 40 paces)
Interface Level: 2
CE: 27 / 400
```

Forty paces. Almost twice what he had yesterday.

I'm eight years old, he thinks. And I just crossed the line that most of the cousins will never cross. The thought gives him no pleasure. It should. It is the thing he has been working toward for two years. But it sits in his chest like a stone, because he knows what it costs, and who paid, and for what.

Layer five, he thinks. Enough to be useful.

He climbs into bed. He does not sleep.

\ \ \*

"Fifth," says Old Hu, the next morning.

He is not looking at Lin Jian. He is looking at the weeds in the cracks of the forge yard, with a bowl of soup in his hand. He says it flatly, as if reading the label on a jar.

"Sir?"

"Your Qi's got a shape to it I haven't seen before. You came through the door like a boy who'd had the lock picked." Hu drinks. "You're eight."

"Yes."

"And before the winter you were at the second." The old man sets down the bowl. "I have taught eleven boys and girls in my life, Jian, and I have never taught one who did that. I won't ask how. But I'm going to tell you what it means."

Lin Jian waits.

"It means," says Hu, "that you are going to be tempted to believe you are something you are not. You are going to see a man at the seventh layer and think, I could beat him. And you may even be right. But he will have a hundred more breaths than you have, and a hundred more tricks, and he won't care that you're eight."

"I know."

"You don't. Not yet." The one eye is steady. "Which is why I'm giving you this."

He reaches behind him, under the bench, and pulls out a long flat leather case. He sets it on the anvil and opens it.

Inside, on a bed of oiled cloth, lies a belt.

It is a plain brown belt, narrow, a child's length. At regular intervals along its inner face run nine narrow sleeves of stitched leather, and in each sleeve is a pin. Dull gray spirit iron, a hand's length, needle-pointed, with a tight spiral running down the shaft. They look exactly like the pins in the pit. They are not.

Lin Jian does not need to touch them. The interface unfolds the instant he looks.

```
[Scan: Nine-Pin Belt]
Grade: Yellow (low)
Pins: 9 spirit iron (mid-grade), spiral groove uniformity 99.6%
Qi channels: double-wound
Modes: 4-pin binding / 6-pin snare / 9-pin pit
Maker's mark: [unreadable — filed off]
Condition: excellent. Not used.
```

A real one. Ninety-nine point six.

"I made it," says Hu, "for a man I couldn't save. Fifteen years ago. Before I came here." His voice is dull and careful. "It's the best thing I ever did with my hand. It's been in the bottom of a chest ever since, and I don't want to look at it again." He pushes the case across the anvil. "So you take it."

Lin Jian does not move.

"Yellow grade, which means it's worth more than anything else in this house except the Patriarch's sword. Do not tell anyone you have it. Not your father. Not your mother. Not your brother, who would want it." The old man's face is rough as a cliff. "When the time comes, you'll know how to use it better than I do. I've watched you work."

"Sir. I can't."

"You can, and you will." The voice cracks like a whip. "I am an old man with one arm and a bad lung and a past that is going to come up that road one day, and when it does I do not want to spend my last hundred breaths wishing I'd given you the damned belt. Take it."

Lin Jian takes it.

It is heavier than it looks, and warm, as though the iron remembers someone's hand. He fastens it around his waist, under his short robe, where no one will see. It fits as if it had been made for him.

"Thank you," he says.

Hu waves a hand. "Don't thank me. Check the pit."

\ \ \*

He checks the pit at sunrise, as he has every morning.

It is not a duty anyone has given him. It is simply a habit, formed in the last few days and as hard to break as any other: walk the north rim before the household wakes, crouch at the gap in the quarry, lay his hand on the gravel, scan. A quick one, half a breath, to be sure nothing has shifted in the night.

This morning, the scan stops him cold.

```
[Scan: Nine-Pin Pit (Quarry Gap)]
Pins: 9, in position
Pin 6 (south): displaced 3.1 mm from original seat; rotated ~4 degrees
Array coherence: 72% (was 86%)
Foreign residue on pin 6: silver-lead compound (trace), organic oil (palm)
Last disturbance: est. 5–7 hours ago
```

Lin Jian does not move.

Somebody has been here. Not an animal. Not weather. Somebody has crouched where he is crouching, in the dark, and put a hand on pin six, and turned it by four degrees, so slightly that Hu's eye would never catch it and the pit would still look perfect, and still hold for sixty breaths instead of a hundred. A weakness no one would find until it was needed.

And they left a smear of silver-lead on the pin, from a hand that had been holding something.

A pencil. A pencil with a silver tip.

He thinks of the silver pencil moving across a page at the council table. He thinks of a quiet round-faced man with soft hands, saying I'll keep the record, Father. He knows exactly how little that is. Half the family writes with silverpoint. It would not hold in front of a child, let alone an arbiter.

Nobody told him about the quarry gap. That is the thing that makes the back of his neck go cold. The five who were there swore it on Grandfather's sword. Which means that either one of those five told him, or someone else watched them go down in the dark, and followed.

He gets up slowly. He walks, very casually, to Hu's forge.

\ \ \*

Old Hu listens in silence.

He stands in the doorway with his arm folded and his jaw set, and when Lin Jian is done he says nothing for a long moment. Then he goes to the bench and pulls out a drawer and takes from it a small jar, the size of a thimble, sealed with wax.

"Dust," he says. "Pale, almost white. Mixed with cinnabar and a pinch of something your father calls glow-salt. Invisible by day. Under a Moonlamp," he shrugs, "it burns like a lantern. I used it once, a long time ago, to find out which of my apprentices was stealing silver."

Lin Jian takes the jar.

"Dust the pins," says Hu. "Underneath. On the buried half, the part nobody has a reason to touch. If anyone but us puts a hand on that pin, it will come away on his fingers, and it will not wash off with a Cleansing slip, not for two days." He gives a grim half smile. "Nobody uses a Cleansing slip on a hand that's been somewhere it shouldn't. They think no one saw."

"What if he doesn't come back?"

"Then he's cleverer than I thought." The old man's eye is as black and bright as a bird's. "And we've lost nothing."

"And if he does?"

"Then we light a lamp," says Old Hu, "and see who's holding it."

That night, under the pale blue moon of a Moonlamp, Lin Jian crouches in the quarry gap and pulls up pin six. He turns it, and dusts the buried half with the white powder, a thin careful ring of it, and sets it back into the earth at its proper angle, to the hair. He does the same for pin four, and pin eight. Then he rakes the gravel smooth.

He goes up the hill and sleeps for two hours.

At dawn he comes down again with the lamp in his hand and a stone in his stomach.

The pit is unchanged. Three of the nine pins have been pulled out of the earth and put back.

He doesn't have to scan. The Moonlamp, held low over the gravel, shows him everything: three faint blue thumbprints on the rim of the ring, and beside them, leading away in a neat line, a set of boot prints glowing softly in the dark, small, rounded, a little pigeon-toed on the left.

The prints go uphill, toward the wall.

Lin Jian follows them with the lamp, step by glowing step, up the terraces and across the herb beds and along the base of the old library wall, to a narrow wooden door set into the stone. A door he knows very well. A door that has three keys, and three keys only.

The prints stop at the sill.

He holds the lamp up. The light picks out, on the iron of the latch, a faint blue smear the shape of a palm.

For a long moment he stands there, in the cold, with the lamp in his hand and the sun coming up gold over the ridge behind him, and does not breathe.

Then he lowers the lamp, and goes to wake his grandfather.
